# Seasons

Here is a question most college graduates get wrong when someone asks it on
camera: why is it hot in summer and cold in winter? Write your answer down.
Pencils are cheap.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- explain the seasons from Earth's tilt, and rule out distance;
- identify the solstices and equinoxes and what happens at each;
- predict the Sun's path and its noon height on a given date.

## Tilt, Not Distance {#the-cause-of-the-seasons}

The favorite answer is that Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. It is a good
wrong answer: closer usually does mean warmer. It just is not what happens.

Two facts end it. First, Earth's orbit is very nearly a circle, and Earth is
**closest** to the Sun, about 147 million km, in early **January**. It is
farthest, about 152 million km, in early July. That is a 3 percent difference,
and it runs the wrong way for the north. Second, when it is summer in the
Northern Hemisphere it is winter in Australia, on the same day, at the same
distance from the Sun.

The real cause is the **tilt**. Earth's axis is tilted 23.5 degrees, and it
keeps pointing the same direction in space all year, toward Polaris. Around
June the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun; around December it leans
away. The axis does not flip. Earth moves to the other side of the Sun.

Leaning toward the Sun does two things, and both warm you up:

1. **The sunlight arrives more directly.** Shine a flashlight straight down on
   a table: a small, bright circle. Tilt it: the same light spreads into a
   big, dim oval. High summer Sun is the straight beam; low winter Sun is the
   tilted one. Same energy, more area, less heating per square meter.
2. **The days are longer.** At 47 degrees north there are about 16 hours of
   daylight in June and about 8.5 in December.

## Solstices and Equinoxes {#solstices-and-equinoxes}

Four dates mark the year:

| Date (about) | Name | The Sun | Northern Hemisphere |
|---|---|---|---|
| June 21 | June solstice | farthest north, over 23.5 degrees N | longest day |
| September 22 | September equinox | over the equator | 12 hours of day |
| December 21 | December solstice | farthest south, over 23.5 degrees S | shortest day |
| March 20 | March equinox | over the equator | 12 hours of day |

*Solstice* means "the Sun stands still": its noon height stops climbing (or
falling) and turns back. At the equinoxes, day and night are about 12 hours
each everywhere on Earth.

The same 23.5 degrees shows up on every world map. The Tropics of Cancer and
Capricorn, at 23.5 degrees north and south, are as far from the equator as the
Sun can be straight overhead. The Arctic Circle, at 66.5 degrees north, is
where the Sun does not set at the June solstice.

The solstice is not the hottest day. Oceans and land take weeks to warm up, so
the hottest weather comes in July or August: a pot keeps heating after you
turn the burner down.

## The Sun's Path Across the Sky {#the-suns-path}

Every day the Sun follows an arc from east to west. In summer the arc is long
and high; in winter it is short and low. One rule gives its height at noon:

> noon altitude = 90 degrees - latitude + the Sun's declination

The declination is +23.5 degrees at the June solstice, 0 at the equinoxes,
and -23.5 degrees at the December solstice. At latitude 47 degrees north:
June gives 90 - 47 + 23.5 = 66.5 degrees; December gives 19.5 degrees. That is
why winter shadows are so long.

Where the Sun rises moves too. At the equinoxes it rises due east and sets
due west, everywhere. In northern summer it rises north of east and sets north
of west; in winter it rises south of east and sets south of west.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it this week"}
Pick a landmark you can see to the west: a tree, a roofline, a hill. Note
where the Sun sets compared with it. Do it again two weeks later. The sunset
point slides along the horizon, faster near the equinoxes than near the
solstices. That is observing log entry 3.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="b">
  <div class="question">1. In early January Earth is at its closest to the Sun. What season is it in Sydney, Australia?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> Winter, because it is January</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> Summer, because the Southern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> Summer, because Earth is closest to the Sun</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> Spring, because it is halfway between solstices</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>b</strong>. The tilt decides the season. Distance does not: the north has winter at the same moment, at the same distance.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="c">
  <div class="question">2. At latitude 40 degrees north, how high is the noon Sun at the equinoxes?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> 40 degrees</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> 26.5 degrees</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> 50 degrees</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> 73.5 degrees</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>c</strong>. 90 - 40 + 0 = 50 degrees. In June it would be 73.5 degrees.
  </div>
</div>
```

## Where this fits

The seasons use the same skill as the phases: what you see depends on where
things sit relative to the Sun. Next: light, and the instruments that collect it.
